Prison,...
We have ever heard at least 1 story or rumor about this place called prison,
if it wasn't bar-talk, it was from an acquaintance who had to serve out time.
One of the last places most of us ever want to end up in,
still, some call this place at home or even a hotel,
for some the last stop or also a long period close enough to call it hell on earth,
if we can trust the justice system then we can rest assured that the people whose prison life is hell on earth, often rightfully deserve this.
Yet there are people who take on a job on a voluntary or purposeful basis in a prison, it requires that there is a ranking system above the inmates, areas where people who committed all possible crimes sit together and watch TV still requires a fair amount of eyes and order .
And this is where your responsibility begins.

Early Access Gameplay: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5HmEofuzJwQ

In Prison Simulator you will be responsible for many tasks,
prison life is often rough, but often you decide how rough,
Are you going to be a crooked guard, or are you going to do everything by the book?
There are several gangs present, and in addition to them you will also need to gain respect from non-members, the presence of animosity between the gangs or inmates will also create delicacy issues that may leave you no choice but to close the 'prison guard's manual' to do.
Many reasons that will make the pressure on your fragile civil servant shoulders heavier which can make you as a guard a bigger target for certain prisoners and pay attention because every prisoner has different behavioral characteristics..
You also have different ways to defend yourself and overpower the attackers, violence with your fists, your nightstick, a tazer to even firearms or even a fire extinguisher.

You will be responsible for the order and execution of the daily tasks and daily distribution of both new and current prisoners,
Inspect and 'welcome fresh meat, check attendances, check cells, lead them to their outdoor areas or workshops and make sure they carry out their duties in an exemplary manner.
If they don't, feel free to take steps to force them.
Be on the lookout, because at any moment there can be unrest such as fights, pyromania, or even riots,
other reasons for concern may mean you are the target.
There are therefore ways to reduce this risk by showing tolerance,
You can sometimes follow the rules, but sometimes turning a blind eye is just a little extra comfort for those you think deserve.

You also have stats that you can upgrade through mini games that can be accessed at certain places on the prison grounds,
for example, you can lift weights in the outdoor yard whatever boosts your stamina, or make a bet to throw hoops to earn respect, the shooting range and others.

All in all, Prison Simulator is another comprehensive simulator game that has a lot to deal with and also funny moments,
there is a demo and also a prologue version available on steam of the game if you already want a pre-purchase experience.
Also looking forward to the future VR version of the game ( Prison Simulator VR https://store.steampowered.com/app/1088190/Prison_Simulator_VR/ )
No doubt this will be a successful VR game.

Review of Prison Simulator

Imagine the thrilling daily grind of prison life without the actual risk of losing your freedom—Prison Simulator is here to fulfill that fantasy! This game offers a laugh-out-loud, heart-pounding simulation where you can become either the hero or the villain of the penitentiary.

From the moment you step into the shoes of a prison guard, you're greeted with a world where every decision can make or break your reputation. Will you maintain order and become the best guard the prison has ever seen? Or will you stumble into the role of the worst scumbag in history, with inmates rolling their eyes at your blunders?

With its unique blend of intense management and hilarious scenarios, Prison Simulator delivers endless entertainment. The VR version adds a layer of immersion that lets you feel like you're actually patrolling the cellblocks, dealing with rowdy inmates, and navigating the trials of prison life. It's not just about managing chaos; it’s about laughing at the absurdity of it all and having a blast while doing so.

Whether you’re strategizing your way through a riot or just trying to avoid stepping on a lunch tray, this game is a must-have for anyone who enjoys a good chuckle and a challenge. Get ready to embrace the wild side of law enforcement with Prison Simulator!

While the game still has some bugs and can load a bit slow on my computer (maybe it needs to be on SSD?)  the premise and execution of the game is interesting. You can customize the prisoners and even import facial masks over the prisoners which is pretty impressive for a game like this. I was expecting some sliders but that addition leads to pretty powerful customization, even if many people may not feel comfortable with it. With workshop integration, the community might be able to create some interesting people to add to the role playing. I hope more things become customizable  in the future. 

The game includes a variety of mini games, such as a "paper please" like document, observing objects for contraband and others like basketball. You can wager against the npcs or you can compare yourself to others on the leader board. Only caveat is that if you want online stats you need to agree to send play data to the developers. 

You can play as a total ass but the game encourages you to behave properly through a ranking system based on npc respect. You can of course choose to ignore this by participating in the black market and deal with riots instead and the possibility of getting fired. 

The game has stats and perks as well, which I wasn't expecting. You can think of those as QOL changes that make your life easier. Leveling up also slowly unlocks other aspects of the jail.

Hopefully we the developer will continue to expand the game as well with other options so it doesn't become too repetitive if played in long bursts.

 Right now I recommend personalizing your inmates so you can roleplay to keep the game interesting, like in the sims. Personally I am going to wait for more optimizations before going deeper in the game or maybe wait until I get a newer PC (I am over the spec requirements but I think they might be too conservative).

I have a pretty good amount of time in this game, and let me say that it's exactly what I was looking for. It's comparable to the Escapists in that you go through the daily routine of a prison, except in this game you're a guard rather than a prisoner. You have to balance the respect of your fellow guards and the prisoners to avoid starting a riot or getting fired, and you do this by deciding whether you should take contraband, punish prisoners for misdoings or make deals with them, as well as by upgrading the prison and winning games that they challenge you to. Every once in a while(in the career mode) there will be events that interrupt your normal schedule and help forward the story's narrative. 

tl;dr: This is a great game for those who enjoyed Escapists or other more monotonous simulator games, the career mode is better for those who want a story that moves as you play, and the freeplay mode is best for those who just enjoy the day-to-day routine.

Prison Simulator, although incredibly silly, has a decent amount of depth to it that makes it very rewarding and dynamic.

In this game, you play as a guard, and can either be law-abiding, or corrupt and self-profiting. You have options in regards to everything. You can be forgiving to prisoners, or unnecessarily cruel (even guards).

Every character has unique behavioral elements that might make them react to different situations in a variety of ways. Fires can break out, as well as fist fights. Prisoners hide contraband in their cells, that if you find, you can either confiscate officially, or keep for yourself, off the record. I loved having the choice. Especially because you have to make sure no one sees you snagging any goods.

On top of the main jobs you have to do throughout the day, there are a lot of side goals to go for, including improving your stats, but the game is so silly and enables you to goof around, that you will create mini stories of your own. This is helped by the fact that you can create your prisoners, which helps you remember and get attached to them. You will grow to be more lenient towards some, while hating others. There were some that I ended up favoring over others.

Although you can be abusive, the game does reward appeasing guards and prisoners. As your average respect goes up, so will your income, which allows you to purchase personal upgrades, as well as additions to the prison, which in turn will further improve guard/prisoner relations and income, as well as give you access to new mechanics like trading goods with prisoners. It's a really satisfying loop!

As for the main quests, I enjoy the routines you do on a daily basis. They switch things up so you aren't always doing the same thing over and over. Although, with a simulation game like this, there is a bit of repetition at some point, but mechanics like upgrades and randomization help it from getting stale. However, some more interesting narrative quests come into play sometimes that shake things up. I really enjoyed them!

To summarize, it's a game that doesn't take itself seriously, but with a reasonable amount of depth and simulation mechanics that make it feel like a real game too. It's really a lot of fun!

🔸 The story part of [i]Prison Simulator[/i] is perhaps kinda linear, I can say that at some points it was going high and higher with the story and then suddenly it all dropped down, felt like the Developers just left the story part of the game and wanted to work on making fun activities which kinda worked for them. The Story of the game begins with a murder in the prison, where you are tasked to find out who is the murderer, upon following clues you finally find him but after some actions taken in-game you find yourself involved in a drug trafficking situation! 

◼️ Sadly most of the story part of the game is just going back and forth talking with a certain prisoner or prison guard then tasked with earning/having X amount of money to buy an item which will progress in the story and unlock a little small amount of clue of what is happening. The game puts you into the role of a prison guard and does this fairly well, though the challenges that arise daily in your shift are probably things that do happen, but rarely in real life. You can be a straight and narrow rule follower or you can indulge in corruption if that's your thing.

Prison Simulator is a tongue-in-cheek first-person management experience that invites players to step into the boots of a correctional officer and navigate the daily grind of life inside a penitentiary. Developed by Baked Games and published by PlayWay S.A. alongside the developer’s own label, the game mixes routine-based simulation with chaotic unpredictability, blending dark humor with bursts of genuine tension. Rather than striving for gritty realism, it leans into a playful and occasionally satirical depiction of prison life. You begin as a rookie guard assigned to a rundown facility, gradually learning the rhythms of inmate movement, contraband inspection, yard duty, and meal supervision. This early phase establishes the game’s central appeal: you are given a job with structure, but what happens within that structure can vary wildly depending on your decisions—and the unpredictable behavior of the inmates.

The day-to-day gameplay consists of completing assigned tasks that mimic the routines of a correctional officer. These include checking cells for forbidden items, managing roll calls, escorting troublesome inmates, breaking up fights, patrolling corridors, and keeping order in shared spaces. Each task is presented as a small interactive scenario, often supported by simple mini-games. While these mechanics are easy to learn, their repetition quickly reveals the game’s sandbox nature; the true engagement comes from how you choose to play your role. You can maintain discipline by the book, enforcing rules strictly and building respect among guards, or you can stray into corruption—taking bribes, overlooking suspicious behavior, or bending the rules for personal gain. This moral flexibility gives the simulation an unexpected layer of role-playing depth, allowing the player to shape the prison’s atmosphere, inmate dynamics, and their own reputation.

Visually, the game presents a drab, utilitarian prison environment that fits the setting while revealing its indie origins. The blocky architecture, repetitive textures, and stiff character animations evoke a modest budget, yet the art direction succeeds in establishing a grimy, oppressive atmosphere. Inmates shuffle, taunt, or erupt into violence with little warning, making the environment feel active even when the visuals lack polish. Technical imperfections remain noticeable: occasional clipping, AI oddities, and uneven sound design remind the player that the simulation is held together by a small team’s ambition. Still, the tone and presentation complement the game’s somewhat exaggerated approach to prison life—bleak enough to support tension, but not so serious that its rough edges feel out of place.

Narratively, Prison Simulator doesn’t revolve around a traditional storyline. Instead, it uses small vignettes, personal interactions, and dynamic events to create a loose narrative that emerges from your actions. Whether you unfairly punish a prisoner, break up a riot, accept a bribe, or earn praise from fellow guards, the game quietly tracks your behavior and adjusts inmate sentiment accordingly. These shifting relationships generate micro-stories: grudges, alliances, brewing unrest, or unexpected moments of calm. The lack of overarching plot frees the game to focus on moment-to-moment unpredictability. Some players may find this approach liberating, while others may crave a more structured or dramatic narrative arc.

Despite its entertaining foundation, the game’s limitations become more apparent over time. Tasks begin to feel routine, and the variety offered early on does not expand enough to sustain long-term depth. The mini-games tied to searches, inspections, or prisoner management can grow repetitive after extended play. The systems, while functional, lack deeper mechanics that might support more complex emergent scenarios or strategic decision-making. As a result, the game’s strongest hours are often the early ones, when its novelty and moral freedom are most impactful. Once you’ve seen the core loops and explored both the lawful and corrupt paths, replayability depends largely on your personal appetite for sandbox role-play rather than evolving mechanics.

In the end, Prison Simulator succeeds as a light, humorous, and accessible take on correctional facility management. It offers enough freedom to let players experiment with different personas—strict enforcer, opportunistic schemer, or indifferent clock-puncher—and its simulated chaos often leads to amusing or tense moments. Though it lacks the depth, polish, and realism of more advanced simulation titles, its charm lies in its willingness to be both silly and slightly subversive. For players seeking a straightforward yet entertaining simulation with a dark comedic edge, it delivers a satisfying experience. For those searching for a deeply layered or highly polished management sim, it may feel too shallow once its initial novelty fades.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

Prison Simulator gives all the power of being a corrupt junior dictator to the player. Take a few bribes, steal prisoner food, and beat down a few people is good work ethic to imitate. The player can be an honest upstanding guard who serves and obeys the law too. But who wants to do that? We are locked in a cage with killers, robbers, corrupt guards, and other malefactors. Might as well be an animal too. 

When someone doesn't obey your orders, just beat the prisoner senseless. He'll learn to obey. To make sure your job is done right, make sure you beat them senseless and throw them into solitary confinement afterwards. Some people will read this and think this is inhumane, what about prisoners' rights? Don't worry, you can taze prisoners instead of beating them. 

The game is very fun but has issues.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]

[b] 6/10[/b]

[h1]Extended Version[/h1]

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]

[*][b]Fun[/b] You can take bribes, beat prisoners and guards, and be ranked one of the top prisons in the land. 

[*][b]Routine[/b] You can patrol the canteen or prison yard. Most routines revolve around watching prisoners closely to make sure they behave. If they don't behave, well you can talk it out or show them what a tazer feels like. 

[*][b]Plot.[/b] The story starts off well....

[/list]

[b]Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*][b]Repetitive[/b]  There is only so many times before patrolling and watching prisoners gets boring. This could of been better, see my next point. 

[*][b]Immersion.[/b] There is none. The devs offer the player an onslaught of tools that have no practical purpose. Players are shown things like respect and who characters dislike. What does the player do with these things? The player may be attacked by the same person every so often. Incidents and conflicts don't seem to build into anything. A fight is just a fight, not a lead to something greater. The devs should of been more imaginative with the tools they offered. If the player is hated by the prisoners, there should be more events that express this. For example, during one of the times when the player is radioed to go somewhere the player should be ambushed by a few prisoners. Or maybe the player should be randomly searched by the prison guards for having illegal items. If the player wants to get too rough beating prisoners, he never gets reprimanded. There are gangs but there is no gang warfare! Many things could of been used better. Come on devs, do better! 

[*][b]Voice Acting and Ambience[/b]  There is mumbling or some noise going on, it's not very engaging. The prison is extremely quiet, doesn't feel like a prison. 

[*][b]The Plot[/b] The ending is anti-climatic and rushed. The developers seemed to hate the game by the end. A string of events that make no sense are shot at the player rapidly. The plot seemed far too short. 
[/list]

This game has a lot of potential and is still being worked on, so this is a 'not recommend' as of this time of this review. This developer deserves a lot of credit for actually reading the reviews on here and responding, so I'll be addressing this review to them for constructive criticism.

From a positive standpoint, this has had way more work and thought put into it than 90% of budget Unity asset games out there now. But that bar is pretty low in my opinion.

I love the options of creating your own prisoners, and having your own custom prisoner population. You can even make prison gangs, and upload your own image of their gang icon! Also the descriptions of the prisoner's history and personalities are hilarious. It seems a lot of the prison inmate population believes the president to be reptilian, and that the world is flat. I hope they expand on the options in the prisoner creation section, as of right now it's just okay on the whole, with no too many options. 

My biggest complaint about the game right now is just that a lot of the gameplay is unnecessarily tedious. I understand that some of this stuff will feel like a chore, because it is, but I see a lot of needless hassle. For example:

-Like in the event where the prisoners are working in the woodshop, you have to take each tool out of the tool kit and hand them individually to each prisoner, then individually take them back and put them away at the end. At least have the prisoners put them away on their own. That way you can still assign tools without the chore of putting them away.

-Also the daily headcount gets pretty old. I'd suggest having the clicker be automatic as you walk past the prisoners outside their cells, that way you can still do the fun part of confronting the prisoners who don't come out of their cells. Maybe this can be un unlockable item, 'auto clicker' or something.

-The one voice everyone has is strange. I'll just leave that point there.

-The gang option really interested me, but the game doesn't really explain what the gangs do and from my (limited) gameplay time I didn't see much impact, it wasn't like the prison gangs were at war or anything. 

-Beating up other guard and prisoners seems to have little impact. In a way this is kind of nice since you can go around beating up everyone you want, but it also becomes really boring since nothing happens. They just wake up from their concussion and pretend like nothing happened. I think something should happen.

-Delegating duties to other guards should be an option, at least some of the time. This could cut out some of the menial tasks like the ones I described above, or like escorting prisoners into solitary confinement. It'd be fun to do the first time or once in a while, but having to escort prisoners to solitary confinement every time just makes me want to pick an easier punishment. 

I'll end on one HUGE positive: No microtransactions! Yes, thank God, and thank this developer.  I'll be checking in from time to time, and may change this review in the future. Sorry about the not-recommend, but that doesn't mean you're still not better than most of the lazy products out there. For that, I didn't ask for a refund so consider that a victory for you.

Prison Simulator puts you in the shoes of a rookie correctional officer early into his career. 

Looks fun on paper. Count inmates, search them and their cells, send them to solitary when they behave poorly, break up fights and put out fires. How exciting, right?

I put 12 hours into this game, I will not be putting anymore. I wanted to give it a chance. It had some merits but after about 6ish hours, you've seen it all.

The game is a buggy, broken mess. It's really hard to get into a game when you are searching packages and escorting people to watch them work in a workshop for the 100th time in a row in the first 6 hours of the game.

There's a story line that is borderline insulting to your intelligence and can be completed in almost no time. There's too many objectives in this game, and I really mean TOO many, that just give a vague "Talk to this person" or "Do this thing" and it gives literally no direction as to where that person or thing is.

This usually isn't a huge deal if you don't mind wandering around the same small map for what seems like forever trying to find "Cory Silverwings" or whatever.

Bringing me to my final point, the prison is small. It's very, very small. It consists of a brown hallway, white hallway, prison yard and an electric chair. If you're just trying to get from one end to the other, you'll do it in about 15 seconds.

Did i get $20 worth out of it? Maybe? Possibly right on the fence of yes and no, leaning towards no more. It wasn't a total waste of time but I wouldn't recommend this game unless it's about $10 dollars or you're a very serious prison enthusiast for some reason.

The main quest line takes a while to unfold. 

Buy this game on sale if you're making the purchase.
